If all these suckers are allowed to grow, the mother plant looses its vigour resulting in lower bunch weight and total yield. Therefore, the suckers should not be allowed to grow near the parent plant till the mother plant commences flowering. Trashing:Removal of undesirable material from the banana field like

total yield. Therefore, the suckers should not be allowed to grow near the parent plant till the mother plant commences flowering. Trashing:Removal of undesirable material from the banana field like dried, diseased and decayed leaves, pseudo stem after harvest, male bud, last end of inflorescence and withered floral parts. Mattocking: After harvest of the bunch, the plant stem should be cut after 30-45 days to facilitate mobilization of the nutrients from the mother to the developing ratoon plant. The pseudo stem should be cut leaving a stump of about 0.6m height. Wrapping of bunches: It is covering of bunches with polythene or gunny cloth that protects the fruits from intense heat, hot wind, etc. toimprove colour of the fruits. Tipping: Process of removal of heart or male bud. It should be cut soon after the bunch is formed, otherwise it is likely to use up some of the food, which would otherwise go to the development of fruits. Removal of floral remnants: The removal of dried and persistent floral remnants present at the apex of the fruit or finger helps in preventing the spread of fungal diseases. These floral remnants provide shelter to some of the fungal spores. Propping: It is a method by which support is given to banana bearing plants with the help of bamboo or eucalyptus poles, protecting them from bending or falling down due to heavy bunch load and from heavy damage by wind. It is essential for tall varieties. Earthing up: It should be done

protecting them from bending or falling down due to heavy bunch load and from heavy damage by wind. It is essential for tall varieties. Earthing up: It should be done during the rainy season to provide drainage and to avoid water logging at the base. It is to be done once in 2 or 3 months to prevent soil erosion from the basins and to avoid direct contact of water with pseudo stem. Weeding: In the first four months after planting, it is necessary to remove weeds. The stirring of the soil by the spade after every 6 or 7 irrigations is necessary to maintain its tilth and absorptive power. Use of Diuron @ 4 kg/ hectare and Simazine @ 6kg/ hectare control grasses and broad leaved weeds when applied after planting and repeated 30 days after planting. Fertilizer application: Banana is a heavy feeder, Due to shallow root system, it responds well to applied nutrients. The high fertilizers requirement is mainly due to their rapid and vigorous growth and high fruit yield. 200-250g Nitrogen, 30-40g Phosphorus, 200-250 g potassium per plant is required. Fertilizers have to be applied before initiation of inflorescence in 3 splits i.e. 2nd, 4th and 6th months after planting. matures in 4-5 months depending upon varieties, climate, etc. • Banana are harvested at 3/4th maturity stage for distant markets or for chips making purpose while, for local markets are harvested at full maturity. • The following are the indications of maturity of banana. • Drying of top leaves. • Changing of fruit colour from green to light green. • The floral ends of fruits are shed with slight hand touch at apices. • Fruit become plumpy and angles are filled & disappear. • One or two fruits ripe at the basal end (yellow colour). • Starch content of the fruit (22-25%). • The bunches are to be harvested by leaving 2 ft of peduncle on the bunch. Storage: • Banana can be stored at 13°C with the Relative Humidity of 85-95 % for 3 weeks • The fruits should not be stored / shifted under refrigerated condition. • The storage life can be increased by keeping the fruits in high concentration of carbon dioxide and low concentration of oxygen. • Also storing in sealed polythene bags containing ethylene

Yield: Yield of banana varies with variety, agroclimatic situation and management practices. Tall cultivars usually yield 15-20 t/ ha. Dwarf varieties yield 30-40 t/ ha. – Management Practices Pomegranate Botanical name: Punica granatum Family: Punicaceae Pomegranate fruit is liked for its cool and refreshing juice besides its use as a table fruit. The juice is considered to be useful for patients suffering from leprosy. The bark and rind of the fruit are commonly used against dysentery and diarrhoea. The rind of the fruit is also a source of dye, which gives yellowish brown colour and is used for dyeing wool and silk. Flowers yield a light red dye used in dyeing clothes. Climate: Pomegranate is mainly subtropical fruit. However; it can adopt to wide range of climatic conditions and can grow up to 1800m above sea level. The tree grows best in semiarid climate where cool winter and hot dry summer prevail. The tree requires hot and dry climate during the period of fruit development and ripening. The optimum temperature for fruit development is 38°C.The tree cannot produce sweet fruits unless the temperature is high for a sufficient long period. Under humid conditions, the sweetness of the fruit is adversely affected. Soils: It can be grown on varied types of soils. The deep loamy or alluvial soils are ideal for its cultivation. It can tolerate slightly alkaline soils. It can thrive well on comparatively poor soils where other fruits fail to grow. It can also be grown in medium and black soils. It

can tolerate slightly alkaline soils. It can thrive well on comparatively poor soils where other fruits fail to grow. It can also be grown in medium and black soils. It is rated as salt-hardy fruit plant. Varieties: The edible part of pomegranate fruit is the juicy outgrowth of the seed called the aril. Good taste, flavour and attractive seed colour (Aril) are favoured by the consumers, but all these characters are not found in any single cultivar. However on the basis of yield and other quality characteristics various varieties have been recommended for commercial cultivation. Ganesh:It is a selection from ‘Alandi’. It has medium sized fruits, aril is pinkish with sweet juice. Seeds are very soft. Fruit surface is smooth, yellow with red tinge, round in shape average fruit weight 325 g. Mridula: Fruits are medium sized, rind smooth, and dark red in colour. Arils are blood red with very soft seed, juicy and sweet taste. It is significantly superior to other commercially grown pomegranates. The fruits weigh between 230-270g. Ruby (Ganesh x Kabul x Yercaud):This was released from IIHR, Bangalore. The fruits resembles like Ganesh variety with reddish brown skin with green stripes on skin, soft seeded with bigger size and red coloured arils and it is a heavy yielder (16-18 t/ha). The other important commercially grown varieties are Bhagwa, Bedhana, Jodpur, Red Dholka, Alandhi, Musket Red, Jalore seedless, Jyothi, Papershell Propagation: Pomegranate plants raised from seed are not uniform and vary widely which are undesirable and hence to

Among the vegetative methods of propagation hard wood stem cuttings, air layering and root suckers are the important methods. Among these methods, Stem cuttings are universally used for raising plants on commercial basis. Mature wood is used for making the cuttings. The plants are usually ready for transplanting within 8-9 months. Land preparation and planting: Land is prepared thoroughly prior to digging of pits. 60-75 cm3 size pits are dug before the onset of monsoon. The plants are planted usually in the beginning of the monsoon in South India. The distance of planting in many improved varieties is 5 X 4 m. However, planting distance of 3 X2.5 m or 4X2 m has been reported to produce high and economic yield of good quality fruits. Training: Pomegranate may be trained as multi-stemmed tree or single stemmed tree. 1. Single-stemmed tree: The single stem is left by removing all the side shoots at the time of planting. Single stemmed tree has tendency to produce less number of shoots. The single stem system has its own disadvantages. The plants have a tendency to produce ground suckers, making the plant bushy. As such it is difficult to train the plant to a single stem. The crop is highly susceptible to stem borer and shoot hole borer. Thus single stem system of training is uneconomical for commercial cultivation. Therefore, multi stem system of training is more prevalent in the country. 2. Bahar Treatment for crop regulation: A fully grown pomegranate has a tendency to bear flowers and fruits throughout the year. Owing to this, higher yield is not obtained during any period. Manures and fertilizers: It is a hardy fruit plant, growing successfully in low fertile soils. Both macro and micro nutrients affects its growth, development and productivity. One year old plants should be manured with about 10 kg of FYM and 150 to 200 grams of Ammonium sulphate. Prolonged drought causes hardening of peel. If this is followed by heavy irrigation or rains the pulp grows and peel cracks. Classification of greenhouses: greenhouses are classified based on different

to facilitate microclimate requirement of plants in order to obtain quality produce in a covered structure is known as greenhouse technology. Classification of greenhouses: greenhouses are classified based on different factors such as based on shape, type of cladding material used and environmental control. Considering the environmental control greenhouses are classified as low cost, medium cost and high cost. High cost greenhouses are constructed for cultivation of vegetables and flowers for export purpose. In our region, low and medium cost greenhouses are suitable for successful cultivation. POLICIES- INDIAN FOREST ACT Although the forest management in India has been on a sound footing since 1864, the condition of the forests continued to deteriorate through over exploitation. Efforts were made to conserve the forest resources when the policies were formulated. Forest policy promotes actions of a Government for the preservation, maintenance, enhancement of forests and the optimum utilization of forest resources to attain national welfare. The first effort in this direction was made by enunciating the first forest policy of India in India on 19th, October, 1894. The important features of this policy: 1. The state forests are to be administered for the benefit of the public. 2. Forests on hill slopes may be protected. 3. Whenever an effective demand for cultivable land exists, the needed land can only be supplied from the forest area without habitation. 4. Royalty for the government must be collected for various facilities enjoyed by people. The main aim of the first forest policy was to collect revenue from the forests and please the local population by granting rights and concessions. There was no intention to improve the forestry management in general. After independence the Government of India, ministry of Agriculture enunciated the second National Forest Policy on 12th May, 1952 on the basis of six dominant needs of the country, 1. The need for evolving a balanced and complementary land use, so that each land allotted should produce most and deteriorate least. a) The need for checking erosion, progressing place along the

need for evolving a balanced and complementary land use, so that each land allotted should produce most and deteriorate least. a) The need for checking erosion, progressing place along the treeless bank areas of rivers and on vast stretches of undulating waste lands leading to ravine formation. b) Denudation in mountain regions on which depends the perennial water supply of the river system. c) Invasions of seas and on coastal tracts and shifting sand dunes. 2. The need for establishing tree lands wherever possible for public use ensuring increasing supplies of grazing, small wood for agricultural implements and in particular of fire wood to release the cow dung as a manure. 3. The need for sustained supply of timber and other forest produce required for defense, industry etc. 4. The need for the realization of the maximum annual revenue. The policy recommends that India should aim at maintaining one third (1/3rd) of its land area under forest. But this policy mainly aims at conservation forestry and there is no emphasis on production forestry. Therefore to make the existing forest with their low productivity should be converted into plantation forestry of high productivity which is possible only through enunciation of new forest policy of 1988, which has been announced in the parliament by the Minister of Environment, Government of India, on 7th December, 1988. The following factors influence the site for a nursery: Soil: Soil is the most important factor especially the physical properties of soil plays role than that of chemical properties for successful production of plants. The fertile and well drained soils with sandy loam texture, good tilth, medium to small blocky structure, pH varying from 5.5 to 7.5, organic content at least of 2.5% should always be preferred for nursery sites. Deep digging of clay soils is necessary since these do not have the proper permeability and porosity. The site should be quite free from stones, pebbles or coarse gravel as these restrict the root distribution. Water supply: Sustained supply of water throughout the year must be available at the site. Alkaline and polluted water should not be used for watering plants. LECTURE -19 WIND BREAKS AND SHELTER BELTS- IMPORTANT POINTS- TYPE OF PLANTING- ADVANTAGES The term wind break refers to one or two rows of protective planting of trees whereas shelterbelts is a line of trees or shrubs planted to protect an area, especially a field of crops from fierce weather. Importance of Wind Breaks and Shelter Belts: Windbreaks form efficient soil protection against wind erosion particularly at the time when soil cover is

a field of crops from fierce weather. Importance of Wind Breaks and Shelter Belts: Windbreaks form efficient soil protection against wind erosion particularly at the time when soil cover is not protected by the cultivated plant vegetation cover. Strong winds may cause 70% to 100% of a crop to be lost or damaged. Windbreaks may reduce wind speed by 60 to 80%. Other benefits include the generation of a favourable microclimate for plant development and reduction of wind erosion. As a result of scarce vegetation cover that can alter the movement of wind, dry land areas are predominantly windy. Shelter belts established for the purpose 1) to deflect air currents 2) to reduce the velocity of winds 3) to provide general protection to the leeward areas against the effects of wind erosion 4) to protect the leeward areas from desiccating effects of hot wind. Generally in our country the windbreaks are planted in North – South direction to meet the wind forces from Southwest and Northeast. Properly designed shelterbelts have shown the effect over a distance of 40 times the height of the windbreak. There are two zones in a shelterbelt 1) a triangular quiet zone starting from to of the windbreak and extending near to the ground level of a distance of 8 h (i.e. 8 times the height of the windbreak), where the turbulence velocity fluctuations of wind are reduced and below the values of approach flow. 2) above and downwind of the quiet zone is a wake

of the windbreak), where the turbulence velocity fluctuations of wind are reduced and below the values of approach flow. 2) above and downwind of the quiet zone is a wake zone where the turbulent fluctuations are greater than those in approach flow. The degree of protection offered by a windbreak depends upon the orientation, height, density, species composition and spacing of the windbreak. 1) Orientation: To achieve maximum effectiveness, windbreaks should be oriented as close to perpendicular (90 degrees) to the prevailing or problem winds as possible. To allow for changes in wind direction windbreaks are often planted I multiple directions such as L, U or E shapes. 2) Height: A windbreak protects a distance from 2 to 10 times it’s height. So a 5 m high windbreak would protect a distance up to 50 meters away. The best windbreaks are multi-layered comprising various trees to block wind at multiple heights. 3) Density: The density of a windbreak determines how effective it is at reducing the speed of the wind. Moderately dense windbreaks significantly reduce the wind velocities (50-60%). Windbreaks with lower densities are generally ineffective for most crop protection purposes. The moderately dense windbreaks do not cause, as much downwind turbulence as dense windbreaks, hence they are more effective. 4) Species selection: The most desirable plants for a variety of field windbreaks are those that have a density of about 50-80% in single row planting. Their spread not exceeding 3 m and should and should have a potential height

of field windbreaks are those that have a density of about 50-80% in single row planting. Their spread not exceeding 3 m and should and should have a potential height of 5-30 m. Tall, narrow crowned species usually provided the greatest benefit for the amount of land taken out of production. Casuarina, Eucalyptus, Sesbania, Parkinsonia aculeate are highly suitable wind breaks. 5) Spacing: In general, within the row spacing is 1 - 2.5 m for shrubs, 1.5 – 2.5 m for small trees, 2 – 6 m for medium to tall trees. Normally the spacing between the rows varies from 2-6 m. Characteristics of tree species suitable for wind breaks 1. Resistance to drought. 2. Resistance to frost and wind throw i.e., should be deep rooted. 3. Tolerance to temperature extremes. 4. Easy to establish and long lived. 5. Fast growing with tall uniform shape. 6. Resistance to pests and diseases. 7. Should not serve as alternate host for fungi, insects and other pests. Advantages of windbreaks and shelterbelts: 1. LECTURE -20 AGROFORESTRY- DEFINITION- TYPES- ADVANTAGES Agroforestry is a sustainable land management system which increases the overall yield of the land, combines the production of crops (including tree crops) and forest plants and /or animals simultaneously or sequentially on the same unit of land and applies management practices that are compatible with the cultural practices of the local population (King & Chander, 1978). Thus agro-forestry system is an integrated system in which the cultivator works in a tree- crop-livestock system. It is symbiosis of tree growing, crop production and livestock raising none of the practices being detrimental to any other, but in fact often being complementary and beneficial to each other. It is a form of multiple land use for maximization of production for the diverse requirements of rural communities. Need of Agro-forestry: Agro-forestry

Need of Agro-forestry: Agro-forestry is a multiple and intensive land use both for the forest areas and agricultural lands. Planting trees on agricultural fields have the usual benefits by reduction of soil erosion, run-off and floods and moisture conservation which in turn has benefits for crop production. The productivity of soils is also improved through recycling of nutrients by leaf –litter. The nutrient status of the soil is improved or kept in a balanced state as the trees and agri-crops have different demands of nutrients both in space and time. Important benefits to farm community will be release of cow dung for the agricultural land with the increased availability of fuel wood by agro-forestry techniques. The cattle will get fodder, in all seasons, thereby increasing milk yield of milch cattle and motive power of drought animals. Agro-forestry will also provide additional employment opportunities and result in increased source of income. Agro-forestry systems are sustainable in drought prone areas where small and marginal farmers are unable to increase their income. During drought years, when grain yield reduces to a minimum, especially under rainfed conditions, trees in the field generate produce for sustenance of the farmer and his cattle. Based on temporal arrangement of crops: On the basis of crop rotation systems it is again classified as two types. This system includes all agro-forestry systems/ types where annual food or cash crops are alternated with tree crops over time. The two types under this are: a. Shifting cultivation: Practice of shifting cultivation is said to be as old as agriculture itself (Mayer, 1980), when man changed from the food gathering to food production habits. The practice consist in clearing of forests, setting fire to the felled material after it becomes dry and raising agricultural crops for one or more years, followed by a fallow period (8-10 years). Meanwhile, forest trees are rejuvenating the soil and get it ready for the next cycle of burning and cropping. Continued soil fertility depends on the return of vegetative detritus to the surface and the assimilation of the litter breakdown products by the soil. In the past, this cultivation system was well adapted to environment under certain socio-economic conditions of the tribal people. However, with the increase of population and diminishing carrying capacity of forest lands this use has lost its relevance and become a menace. B. Taungya system: Taungya system is the modification of the shifting cultivation in which trees are grown in conjunction with agricultural crops. Taungya system is the modification of the shifting cultivation in which trees are grown in conjunction with agricultural crops. It differs slightly from shifting cultivation regarding, i) there is a temporary overlap between the crops ii) trees in crops during the follow consists of systematically spaced and selected tree species under taungya system. This system was first evolved in Burma in 1980 and this first modern agro-forestry practice. The main aim of this system is afforestation of open lands with a low cost governmental approach. Farmers are temporarily allotted government lands and contracted to plant desired tree species while the trees are young and before the canopy closure (1-3 years) or shade becomes too dense. The farmers are allowed to plant food crops the yield of which becomes their entirely and is regarded as their compensation for planting trees. When food crop is no longer possible due to shading, the farmers are transferred to another open area where they repeat the process. A large variety of crops and trees depending on the soil and climatic conditions are grown. Meanwhile the abandoned area is by then a well established forest and will not be cultivated for annual food crop again until the planted area reaches the maturity and is harvested. II. A. Border Tree Plantations: planting trees along the border of a crop (plot) is known as border tree plantations. This border trees act as fence, protects the crop from wind and fire hazards. Additionally these trees produce green manure as organic matter, fodder for farm animals and produce fire wood. B. Alternate strip or Alternate row planting: each strip consists of two or more rows and is known as Alley cropping or Avenue Corridor Zonal Cropping or Hedge row cropping. When positioned across the slopes and along the contours they are found most effective for erosion control and slope stabilization. Most modern agroforestry system being advance through government programmes are of these two sub systems and the multiple objectives are food, fodder production and site stabilization. They are more favored agroforestry system because the rows act as contour hedge rows which help in stabilization and conserve soil on slopes and act as terracing. They are easy and less laborious to undertake. If the trees planted are nitrogen fixing and are able to generate by coppicing they would serve as a steady source of organic manure to rehabilitate degraded sites. C. Random mix: this method does not follow any specific or orderly placement of the component crops while the arrangement appears in utter confusion, the plants actually their own special ecological nich and are able to coexist very well. In paper industry, wood represents about 30 to 50 % of the total production cost. The conventional source of cellulose fibres for paper has been softwoods (pine, spruce, fir etc.) and hardwoods (Shorea robusta, Madhica latifolia, Casuarina equisetifoila, Boswellia serrata). Conversion of raw material into paper involves a number of steps. The first important step is to achieve separation of cellulose fibres, which in turn are converted into paper mat. In chemical separation of cellulose fibres, over 50 percent material goes into solution. This spent liquor contains uncooked chemicals and organic matter which is mainly lignin. In an integerated mill this spent liquor is processed to recover cooking chemicals and heat, on which is based the entire economics of the process. The pulp is processed to run on a paper machine for conversion into paper. The physical strength of paper and runnability depends upon the fibre characteristics. It therefore, can be seen that the properties of raw material both physical and chemical, have basic bearing on end product quality and overall processing. LECTURE -24 ASHWAGANDHA Scientific Name: Withania somnifera Family: Solanaceae Common Name: Ashwagandha, Penneru gaddalu Ashwagandha is an important medicinal crop of India. Due to the presence of several types of alkaloids it is used as important source of drug in ancient Ayurvedic literature. Its roots contain the alkaloid ‘Withanine A’ and ‘Withanine B’ and Somniferine have the potential use in many ayurvedic and unani preparations. Uses: • Green berries are the rich source of amino acids. Fruits and seeds are diuretic in nature. • Leaves are reported to possess anti helmenthic and febrifuge properties. An infusion of leaves is given for fevers. For the treatment of piles, a decoction of the leaves is used both internally and externally. • Roots have the property of antibiotic and antitumor. Roots are mostly used for curing general and sexual debility. • The leaf paste is used for curing inflammations of tubercular glands and that of roots for curing skin diseases, bronchitis and ulcers. • Ahwagandha is used as medicine for all the age groups. Hence it is known as Indian Ginseng. Distribution: Ashwagandha is found wild in grazing grounds and forest lands of Madhya Pradesh, foothills of Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Western Uttar Pradesh. Its cultivation has been reported in Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan and Punjab. Description

grazing grounds and forest lands of Madhya Pradesh, foothills of Punjab, Himachal Pradesh and Western Uttar Pradesh. Description of the Plant: Ashwagandha is an erect, herbaceous, evergreen, tomentose shrub, all parts are clothed with whitish, stellate hairs. Branching is extensive, the leaf is ovate, entire, thin, its base is cuneate and is densely hairy beneath. The flowers are bisexual, greenish, axillary, in clusters forming umbellate cymes. Fruits turn ornge-red in colour when they mature. Soil: it grows successfully in sandy loam or light red soils with organic matter and drainage. A soil pH range of 7.5 to 8.0 is ideal. Climate: Ashwagandha prefers a subtropical climate grows luxuriantly in areas receiving rainfall of 65-70 cm. It is planted during the late rainy season and prefers dry weather for its successful growth. Varieties: Jawahar Ashwagandha -20, Poshita, rashmita and Nagore. Cultivation: Propagation: It is propagated through seed. The crop can be grown by direct sowing into the field as well as by raising seedlings and transplanting them. The inflorescence is umbellate and hairy, flowers are bisexual. Varieties: Algerian or Tunisian: This type of geranium is slender with flowers of a dark pink colour. It is being grown in the Nilgiris and is unsuitable for wet conditions. This variety yields 50-60% more oil with a more delicate odour than that of Reunion type. Reunion or Bourbon: Grown in the Niligiris and Anamalais, the plant is more sturdy with light pink flowers and more suitable for wet conditions. The oil content is higher during summer months.
